text: 3 Measuring Performance Upper Bounds with Oracles

Let us denote a KG as [MATH \mathcal{K}=(\mathcal{E},\mathcal{R},\mathcal{T})], where [MATH \mathcal{E}] is a set of entities, [MATH \mathcal{R}] a set of relations, and [MATH \mathcal{T}\subseteq\mathcal{E}\times\mathcal{R}\times\mathcal{E}] a set of triples encoding facts. Each triple [MATH (h,r,t)] consists of a head entity [MATH h], a relation [MATH r], and a tail entity [MATH t], e.g., [MATH (\text{France},\text{hasCapital},\text{Paris})]. In link prediction, [MATH \mathcal{T}] is partitioned into fixed training ([MATH \mathcal{T}_{\text{train}}]), validation ([MATH \mathcal{T}_{\text{val}}]), and test ([MATH \mathcal{T}_{\text{test}}]) sets. Given a test triple [MATH (h,r,t)\in\mathcal{T}_{\text{test}}], the task consists in predicting the missing entity in queries of the form [MATH (h,r,?)] or [MATH (?,r,t)] by scoring and ranking all entities, such that the ground-truth entity is ranked as highly as possible. Performance is thus evaluated using rank-based metrics such as Mean Rank (MR), Mean Reciprocal Rank (MRR), and Hits@[MATH K] (typically [MATH K\in\{1,3,10\}]).

In the literature, several models have been proposed to address this task; in this work, we restrict our study to a subset of models denoted [MATH \mathcal{M}]. The training of a model depends on the chosen architecture, a hyperparameter configuration that is often chosen as the one maximizing the rank-based metrics on the validation set, and a random seed to control stochastic factors such as negative sampling or embedding initialization. We call a trained model given these characteristics an instance, that we formally define as follows:
Definition 1 (Instance)

An instance [MATH I=Instance(M,\mathcal{T},\boldsymbol{C},\mathfrak{S})] corresponds to a model [MATH M\in\mathcal{M}] trained on dataset [MATH \mathcal{T}] with hyperparameter configuration [MATH \boldsymbol{C}] and random seed [MATH \mathfrak{S}]. When unambiguous, we write [MATH I_{M}^{\mathfrak{S}}].

Even with [MATH \mathcal{M}], [MATH \mathcal{T}], and [MATH \boldsymbol{C}] fixed, training is stochastic: the learned representations depend on the random seed [MATH \mathfrak{S}] [20]. In standard practice, different instances obtained with distinct seeds are commonly treated as interchangeable, since aggregate link prediction metrics usually exhibit only limited variation across runs [20]. Consequently, experimental results are often reported from a single run or averaged over a few runs, and the specific influence of the seed is largely disregarded.

However, prior work has shown that such instances can yield divergent predictions [20, 36]. This phenomenon can be illustrated in Figure 1, where two instances of Model 1 achieve the same MRR (0.4), yet differ at the query level: the first instance ranks the first query correctly while the second does not, and the opposite holds for the second query. As previously introduced, this variability motivates the use of an ensemble of models to benefit from the different knowledge captured by the different instances [30].

In our work, we further investigate the performance gain brought by such groups of models. To address the two settings of in-model and cross-model complementarity, we consider groups of models that can involve instances of the same model (Definition 2), or instances of different models (Definition 3), respectively.
Definition 2 (Model Group)
Let [MATH M\in\mathcal{M}] be a model. A model group associated with [MATH M] is a finite set of independently trained instances of [MATH M]:
where each instance [MATH I_{M}^{\mathfrak{S}_{i}}] is obtained using a different random seed [MATH \mathfrak{S}_{i}].
Definition 3 (Cross-Model Group)
Let [MATH \mathcal{M}^{\prime}\subseteq\mathcal{M}] be a set of models. A cross-model group is any finite set of instances of models in [MATH \mathcal{M}^{\prime}]:
To characterize the theoretical performance upper-bound of such groups, we model their theoretical best performing behavior as an oracle formally defined as follows.
Definition 4 (Oracle)
Let us denote [MATH \mathcal{Q}] the set of queries. Given a group [MATH G], the oracle associated with [MATH G] is the mapping
where [MATH rank(I,q)] returns the rank assigned by instance [MATH I] to the ground-truth entity for a query [MATH q].

In other words, the oracle can be interpreted as a pseudo-instance that, for each query, achieves the best rank obtained by the instances in [MATH G]. For clarity, we denote the oracle of a model group [MATH G_{M}] or a cross-model group [MATH G_{\mathcal{M}^{\prime}}] as [MATH \mathcal{O}_{M}\equiv\mathcal{O}_{G_{M}}] and [MATH \mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{M}^{\prime}}\equiv\mathcal{O}_{G_{\mathcal{M}^{\prime}}}], respectively.

Figure 1 provides examples of oracle predictions for Model 1. For the first query, the oracle selects the first instance, which ranks the ground-truth entity higher than the second instance ([MATH 1] vs. [MATH 10]). The opposite occurs for the second query. For the third query, both instances yield identical ranks, and the oracle selection is therefore arbitrary. The same procedure applies to Model 2. Figure 1 also illustrates cross-model group oracles with 2 and 4 instances per group. The selection mechanism remains identical, but the oracle can now choose among instances from different models. For example, [MATH \mathcal{O}^{4}_{\mathcal{M}}] will first select instance 1 and then instance 2 from Model 1, and then select the prediction of instance 1 from Model 2, which ranks higher than the Model 1 instances ([MATH 2] vs. [MATH 10]).
This pseudo-instance interpretation allows us to evaluate [MATH \mathcal{O}_{G}] using the same metrics as for standard instances. In particular, the Mean Reciprocal Rank of the oracle is defined as

[MATH \mathrm{MRR}_{\mathcal{O}_{G}}] therefore represents the upper-bound performance achievable if, for each query, one could a priori select the best-performing instance in [MATH G]. This upper-bound thus characterizes the theoretical performance limit of a group of instances w.r.t. perfect prediction, and enables to assess the gap between instances and this upper-bound, paving the way toward enhanced strategies for result aggregation.

To illustrate, in Figure 1, although the instances of Model 1 and Model 2 individually obtain MRR values of [MATH 0.40] and [MATH 0.44], respectively, the collective performance measured by the oracle is higher. In particular, two instances of Model 1 can jointly achieve an MRR of [MATH 0.70], while Model 2 reaches [MATH 0.50]. When combining the first two instances of Model 1 and Model 2, the resulting group achieves an MRR of [MATH 0.61], and this value further increases to [MATH 0.83] when considering the full set of instances.
4 Experimental Settings
Models.

Finally, the complete set of models considered in this work is defined as:

For model implementation, we rely on reference frameworks and implementations, depending on model availability and in decreasing order of priority: LibKGE [5] (for TransE, DistMult, ComplEx, ConvE, RotatE, and RESCAL), PyKEEN [2] (for BoxE), TorchDrug11 1 https://github.com/DeepGraphLearning/torchdrug (for NBFNet and NeuralLP), PyClause [3] (for AMIE and AnyBURL). Finally, we use the original implementation of MINERVA [7], as it is not available in the aforementioned frameworks. Note that the original implementation of MINERVA trains exclusively for tail prediction. To allow comparison with the other considered models, we choose to report results for both head and tail prediction. Specifically, we reformulate each head-prediction query [MATH (?,r,t)] as the equivalent tail-prediction query [MATH (t,r^{-1},?)]. This formulation for head prediction is valid since MINERVA learns to navigate the graph using both relations and their inverses. Also note that AMIE is included in cross-model comparisons, but differs fundamentally from the other approaches as it relies on a fully deterministic rule mining process.
Datasets.

We consider three standard datasets from the literature: WN18RR [8], a subset of the lexical KG WordNet characterized by its hierarchical structure; and FB15k-237 [26] and CoDEx-S [23], derived from Freebase and Wikidata, respectively, two prominent Web KGs containing large collections of real-world facts. We use the standard splits of these datasets, with PyKEEN’s filtering to remove test triples involving entities unseen during training, which removes [MATH 28] out of [MATH 20,466] test triples from FB15k-237, [MATH 210] out of [MATH 3,134] from WN18RR, and none from CoDEx-S.
Instances.

For each [MATH (\text{model},\text{dataset})] pair, we train [MATH 20] independent instances using random seeds ranging from [MATH 0] to [MATH 19]. Instances that fail to converge, defined as achieving a validation MRR strictly below [MATH 0.05], are discarded from the analysis. Consequently, we exclude [MATH 1], [MATH 9], and [MATH 9] NeuralLP instances on WN18RR, FB15k-237, and CoDEx-S, respectively.

For TransE, DistMult, ComplEx, ConvE, RotatE, and RESCAL, we use the official configurations provided in the LibKGE repository for FB15k-237 and WN18RR. These configurations result from the hyperparameter tuning procedure conducted by Ruffinelli et al. [22]. For CoDEx-S, we use the configurations provided in the same repository for TransE, ComplEx, and ConvE, obtained following the hyperparameter tuning procedure as in Safavi et al. [23]. As no dataset-specific configurations are provided for DistMult and RotatE on CoDEx-S, we reuse their FB15k-237 configurations, given the similarity between the two datasets.

For BoxE, MINERVA, and NBFNet, we follow the same principle. We use the official configurations provided by their respective authors for FB15k-237 and WN18RR [1, 7, 37], and reuse the FB15k-237 configurations for CoDEx-S. For NeuralLP, we use the same configuration across all datasets, following the configuration provided in the official TorchDrug tutorial22 2 https://torchdrug.ai/docs/tutorials/reasoning.html.
Finally, AnyBURL and AMIE, implemented with PyClause, are run using the framework’s default configurations.
Evaluation Metrics.

To evaluate instance performance, we focus on the standard Mean Reciprocal Rank (MRR), Hit@1 and Hit@10 metrics. We use filtered ranks, removing all other known true triples from the candidate set, and the pessimistic tie convention, assigning tied candidates the worst rank in their tie group.
Experimental Protocols.
We devise specific experimental protocols to answer each of the research questions.

RQ1 (Section 5.1). For each model [MATH M\in\mathcal{M}], we consider its associated group [MATH G_{M}] composed of [MATH 20] independently trained instances. We compare the average performance across instances, [MATH \overline{\mathrm{MRR}}_{G_{M}}], with the oracle performance over the group, [MATH \mathrm{MRR}_{\mathcal{O}_{M}}].

RQ2 (Section 5.2). We evaluate the performance of cross-model groups. To ensure a fair comparison with single-model groups, we control the total number of instances. Specifically, we sample the same number of instances from each model in a given family [MATH \mathcal{M}^{\prime}], such that the total number of selected instances [MATH k] remains close to [MATH 20]. The corresponding oracle performance is denoted [MATH \mathrm{MRR}^{k}_{\mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{M}^{\prime}}}]. As this sampling is stochastic, we repeat the process [MATH 100] times and report the average oracle performance.

To relax the uniform allocation constraint, we construct a group of [MATH 20] instances using a greedy procedure over [MATH \mathcal{M}], iteratively selecting the instance that yields the largest increase in oracle performance, regardless of its model. Once the greedy procedure is completed, we repeatedly sample new instances while preserving the model proportions of the selected group. This allows us to disentangle the effect of the resulting model allocation from that of the particular instances selected during the greedy procedure, and thus assess whether the observed gain is attributable to a promising model allocation rather than to specific instances. We perform [MATH 100] such samplings and report the resulting average oracle performance as [MATH \mathrm{MRR}^{20,\text{greedy}}_{\mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{M}}}].

RQ3 (Section 5.3). We analyze how oracle performance evolves as the number of instances increases. Given the instances of a group [MATH G], we evaluate [MATH \mathrm{MRR}^{k}_{\mathcal{O}_{G}}] for [MATH k\in\{1,\dots,|G|\}] by progressively considering subsets of size [MATH k]. Since the results depend on the order in which instances are added, we sample [MATH 100] random permutations and report the average oracle performance for each value of [MATH k].
